To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) branch vulnerability to embomism depends on other components of the plant hydraulic network, and (b) the ratio of root to leaf area and root vulnerability to embolisms are more important than branch vulnerability to maintain hydraulic integrity along the soil-to-root continuum.

the coordination of hydraulic traits along the soil-to-canopy continuum is crucial to understand plant water relations and that the vulnerability of the root-to-leaf hydraulic continuum is better regulated through root hydraulic properties and root-to-lead area ratios than branch hydraulic properties.

(i) the vulnerability to embolisms of branches is strongly influenced by the vulnerability of roots and by the ratio of root to leaf area; (ii) the stringency with with which species regulate leaf water potential also influences vulnerability of branches; (iii) the vulnerability of the whole plant is strongly influenced by root vulnerability, root to leaf area ratio, and soil texture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the coordination of hydraulic traits along the soil to leaf continuum.
the integration of hydraulic traits across the whole plant, and how this integration is influenced by environmental factors.
understanding how the whole-plant hydraulic system is integrated and how the system is coordinated to maintain hydraulic function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

plant species have a range of strategies for dealing with the risk of xylem embolism, and the best way to predict how a plant will function under future climate change is to understand the whole plant.
plant hydraulics is a complex and highly dynamic system, and that we are only beginning to unravel it.
the hydraulic architecture is a dynamic yet vulnerable pipeline.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vulnerability of a plant to hydraulic failure is determined by the integration of hydraulic traits throughout the plant.
the whole plant is a dynamic and vulnerable pipeline.
plant hydraulics is a complex, yet vulnerable pipeline that needs to be understood across scales to fully understand plant function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vulnerability curve is a useful tool for understanding plant functioning, but it is not sufficient to describe plant hydraulic function.

the vulnerability of the whole plant to hydraulic failure is not determined by a single component of the hydraulic pathway, but is a function of integration of hydraulic traits along the soil-to-atmosphere continuum.
the vulnerability of a branch depends on the vulnerability of the entire plant and that the whole-plant hydraulic architecture is a dynamic and vulnerable pipeline.
